The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "Introducing the Live Music Analyst": https://pudding.cool/2021/02/jukebox/
The files: data/songlist_wide_optimized.csv, data/track_name_dictionary.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data folder and reading the story.

# Introducing the
# Live Music
Analyst
by Kat Wilson and Kevin Litman-Navarro
It’s been a long time since we’ve seen live music. Of course, with modern streaming platforms, there’s more than enough recorded music to keep us safely locked down ad infinitum; yet there remains a deficiency in our musical diets amidst the plague of cancelled shows and closed venues.
What exactly do we miss? Is it the random banter outside of the lyrics we know by heart? A slow jam revived as an up-tempo frenzy? The spontaneous, five-minute guitar solos? A banger gone acoustic? Or the solidarity of strangers in the audience who love that band as much as you do? Maybe it’s the surrounding context of the show (Johnny Cash’s prison performances, Nirvana’s intimate NYC acoustic set, or LCD Soundsystem’s “final goodbye” Madison Square Garden show), that give us insight into what was going on with the audience, the artist, and the world, at the time of the performance.
In the time before we can go back to crowding Brooklyn Steel or catching an intimate set at Hole in the Wall, we decided to dive into the vast discography of live-recorded albums to try and satiate the desire to catch a show. First, we found as many live albums as we could and matched them to their studio counterparts using the SpotifyAPI. Then, by looking at the differences between live and studio songs using numerical metrics like energy (how intense or lively a track sounds), valence (a measurement of a song’s mood), and duration (to find those five-minute guitar solos), we found great live performances that we had missed.
For instance, Bob Dylan’s Blowin’ in the Wind doesn’t exactly come to mind as the encore to end a cross country stadium tour. The folk ballad is typically sung at a slow, ticking rate; it sounds almost like a lullaby. Dylan metronomically recites the lyrics over a simple acoustic strumming pattern, only pausing for a short, intimate, harmonica break in the middle. When analyzing the data, we noticed that the live-recorded version of the song, off of Before the Flood, is, by contrast, a frenzied, five-minute celebration.
# Blowin' In the Wind — Song Characteristics
Loading data...
Recorded at the Los Angeles Forum during the tail end of Dylan’s 1974 American tour with The Band, the artist (and the audience) take on a new energy. Listen to the difference below.
In this version, fans cheer, and the drums pick up in the background as you hear Dylan’s voice creak over the mic. A guitar solo halfway through replaces Dylan’s studio harmonica, and almost ten seconds of applause linger on as he shouts “Thank you, Goodnight!” It’s as if, over the backdrop of a nation closer to the end of the Vietnam War that first inspired the song, the lyrics take on a different tone.
Other changes are more intentional. David Byrne, for instance, made the choice, when recording three live shows at the Pantages theater in Los Angeles with the Talking Heads, to have each musician and instrument come out onto the stage in succession, one at a time. Byrne was inspired by the minimalist Japanese theater, where stage props and actors were portable, to remove the fourth wall. The resulting performance, captured in the documentary film “Stop Making Sense” brings the audience into the music, creating a type of “build up” approach to sound. You can hear this change in songs like “Heaven,” an acoustic, stripped-down version of the original studio recording.
Levels of speech and instrumentals often seesaw in live performance, too. The iconic saxophone solo in Aretha Franklin’s “Respect,” for example, is certainly not the center of attention, as it is in the studio version. Instead, Aretha’s backup singers take more of a central role. At the Filmore West in San Francisco in 1971, the jam starts out with some stage banter, and the tempo picks up way faster than the studio version. The sax solo is almost “rushed” through, and in its place, backup singers bring even more force to the song.
Using this data, we created the Live Music Analysis Tool. You can search for artists, and find the live tracks that stand out the most compared to the studio version. You might even find someone new that you just have to see.

# Methodology
There are an estimated 10,000 artists who have recorded live albums in recording history. One of our conceptual challenges was figuring out how to get a comprehensive list of artists and albums, while still parsing down the data to create a functional tool. Alas, we might have missed your favorite artist, but hope that we struck some sort of comprehensive list, and encourage you to dig for that underground live version you can’t find here. Our list of artists comes from Wikipedia’s list of live recorded albums, compared to the set of Pop/Rock artists who recorded at least one live recorded album by 9/16/2020, as they appear on AllMusic. We pulled the intersected list of artist names (about 10,950) from the Spotify API, and ended up with around 8,000 artists’ Spotify API data. We culled this list of artists by selecting only artists who had charted on the Billboard Hot 100.
Raw SpotifyAPI data includes song level variables such as acoustics, speech levels, and duration of a song, and album level variables such as album name and year recorded. We hard coded a binary indicator of live/studio by identifying tracks with the string “Live” or “Sessions” in the track name or in the album name. We removed tracks with “Commentary”, “Rehearsals”, “Intro”, “Movie Soundtrack”, or “Demos” from the analysis, and only kept artists who had at least 7 recorded live songs, per the previously created variable, as an indicator that live songs are representative of a live album recording, rather than a one off recording.
Using the new binary indicator of live/studio, we matched tracks by track name and artist name. This yielded multiple matches for a single song. For instance, seven live recordings of “Folsom Prison Blues” exist in the data set, and four studio recordings (Mercury Albums, Total Johnny Cash Sun Collection, All About the Blue Train, and I Walk the Line), giving us 28 possible matches to compare among Live to Studio. To cull the data for the project, we scraped the “popularity index” from our original artist list, and kept only the tracks with the highest popularity index. Using this new, parsed down, matched list of live and studio versions, we calculated the difference of audio features (acoustics, duration, instrumentals) from the live to studio version for each track.
Music is in our hearts, and we will be the first ones back at the venues when they open up again. In the meantime, you can support live music during covid by getting your live performance ready for when the stage opens back, or find other ways to support live musicians.

The story is an interactive tool. The findings are largely in the song characteristics for three songs (Blowin' in the Wind, Heaven, Respect). But those numbers may come from the interactive tool which loads data. The data files given are songlist_wide_optimized.csv (differences) and track_name_dictionary.csv (track names). There's no artist names file, no studio values. Hmm.

Wait — the data gives differences per track_name_id and artist_id. The track_name_dictionary maps track_name_studio to track_name_id. So we could find "Blowin' in the Wind" and compute differences. But the story's specific example is the LA Forum 1974 live version vs studio. The differences file has multiple matches (28 possible for Folsom Prison Blues), each row a live/studio match. The story says they "kept only the tracks with the highest popularity index" to cull. The data file may have multiple rows per track_name_id, one per match.

Let's look at the data structure more. Number of artists, track names, difference columns. Also check if there's a "popularity" column? No — only difference columns and track_key, artist_id.

Hmm, the story's findings: mostly descriptions, not numbers. Findings drawn from data:
- Blowin' in the Wind song characteristics table: valence 0.44→0.33 (-0.11), energy 0.10→0.98 (+0.88), speechiness 0.05→0.31 (0.26), tempo 174.87→153.61 (-21.27), acousticness 0.91→0.13 (-0.79), duration 165→272 (107 seconds), liveness 0.06→0.92.
- "the live-recorded version ... is ... a frenzied, five-minute celebration" — duration 272 seconds (~4.5 min).
- "almost ten seconds of applause linger" — not in data.
- "tempo picks up way faster than the studio version" for Respect — but the data doesn't include tempo difference. Actually difference columns: energy, dance, instrumentalness, valence, acousticness, duration, liveness, overall. No tempo, no speechiness. So the Blowin' in the Wind table includes valence, energy, speechiness, tempo, acousticness, instrumentalness, duration, liveness — only some available.

But do we have studio and live absolute values? No, only differences. So cannot reproduce studio 0.44, live 0.33. But difference_valence = -0.11, difference_energy = 0.88, difference_duration = 107000 ms? Wait duration column values like 26235, -56108 — likely milliseconds. 107 seconds = 107000 ms. Let's check.

The main thing: does the data support the differences for Blowin' in the Wind? We need to find the row matching "Blowin' in the Wind" live at LA Forum vs the studio version. But track_name_dictionary maps track_name_studio → track_name_id. Presumably the live track names are not in the dictionary? Let's inspect.

Also artist_id 0... need mapping from artist_id to artist name — not in these files. Hmm, but maybe track_name_dictionary has only track names. Without artist names, identifying Blowin' in the Wind by Bob Dylan may be possible by track name uniqueness? Let's check.

# Live Music

by Kat Wilson and Kevin Litman-Navarro
It’s been a long time since we’ve seen live music. Of course, with modern streaming platforms, there’s more than enough recorded music to keep us safely locked down ad infinitum; yet there remains a deficiency in our musical diets amidst the plague of cancelled shows and closed venues.
What exactly do we miss? Is it the random banter outside of the lyrics we know by heart? A slow jam revived as an up-tempo frenzy? The spontaneous, five-minute guitar solos? A banger gone acoustic? Or the solidarity of strangers in the audience who love that band as much as you do? Maybe it’s the surrounding context of the show (Johnny Cash’s prison performances, Nirvana’s intimate NYC acoustic set, or LCD Soundsystem’s “final goodbye” Madison Square Garden show), that give us insight into what was going on with the audience, the artist, and the world, at the time of the performance.
In the time before we can go back to crowding Brooklyn Steel or catching an intimate set at Hole in the Wall, we decided to dive into the vast discography of live-recorded albums to try and satiate the desire to catch a show. First, we found as many live albums as we could and matched them to their studio counterparts using the SpotifyAPI. Then, by looking at the differences between live and studio songs using numerical metrics like energy (how intense or lively a track sounds), valence (a measurement of a song’s mood), and duration (to find those five-minute guitar solos), we found great live performances that we had missed.
For instance, Bob Dylan’s Blowin’ in the Wind doesn’t exactly come to mind as the encore to end a cross country stadium tour. The folk ballad is typically sung at a slow, ticking rate; it sounds almost like a lullaby. Dylan metronomically recites the lyrics over a simple acoustic strumming pattern, only pausing for a short, intimate, harmonica break in the middle. When analyzing the data, we noticed that the live-recorded version of the song, off of Before the Flood, is, by contrast, a frenzied, five-minute celebration.
# Blowin' In the Wind — Song Characteristics

Recorded at the Los Angeles Forum during the tail end of Dylan’s 1974 American tour with The Band, the artist (and the audience) take on a new energy. Listen to the difference below.
In this version, fans cheer, and the drums pick up in the background as you hear Dylan’s voice creak over the mic. A guitar solo halfway through replaces Dylan’s studio harmonica, and almost ten seconds of applause linger on as he shouts “Thank you, Goodnight!” It’s as if, over the backdrop of a nation closer to the end of the Vietnam War that first inspired the song, the lyrics take on a different tone.
Other changes are more intentional. David Byrne, for instance, made the choice, when recording three live shows at the Pantages theater in Los Angeles with the Talking Heads, to have each musician and instrument come out onto the stage in succession, one at a time. Byrne was inspired by the minimalist Japanese theater, where stage props and actors were portable, to remove the fourth wall. The resulting performance, captured in the documentary film “Stop Making Sense” brings the audience into the music, creating a type of “build up” approach to sound. You can hear this change in songs like “Heaven,” an acoustic, stripped-down version of the original studio recording.
Levels of speech and instrumentals often seesaw in live performance, too. The iconic saxophone solo in Aretha Franklin’s “Respect,” for example, is certainly not the center of attention, as it is in the studio version. Instead, Aretha’s backup singers take more of a central role. At the Filmore West in San Francisco in 1971, the jam starts out with some stage banter, and the tempo picks up way faster than the studio version. The sax solo is almost “rushed” through, and in its place, backup singers bring even more force to the song.
Using this data, we created the Live Music Analysis Tool. You can search for artists, and find the live tracks that stand out the most compared to the studio version. You might even find someone new that you just have to see.

# Methodology
There are an estimated 10,000 artists who have recorded live albums in recording history. One of our conceptual challenges was figuring out how to get a comprehensive list of artists and albums, while still parsing down the data to create a functional tool. Alas, we might have missed your favorite artist, but hope that we struck some sort of comprehensive list, and encourage you to dig for that underground live version you can’t find here. Our list of artists comes from Wikipedia’s list of live recorded albums, compared to the set of Pop/Rock artists who recorded at least one live recorded album by 9/16/2020, as they appear on AllMusic. We pulled the intersected list of artist names (about 10,950) from the Spotify API, and ended up with around 8,000 artists’ Spotify API data. We culled this list of artists by selecting only artists who had charted on the Billboard Hot 100.
Raw SpotifyAPI data includes song level variables such as acoustics, speech levels, and duration of a song, and album level variables such as album name and year recorded. We hard coded a binary indicator of live/studio by identifying tracks with the string “Live” or “Sessions” in the track name or in the album name. We removed tracks with “Commentary”, “Rehearsals”, “Intro”, “Movie Soundtrack”, or “Demos” from the analysis, and only kept artists who had at least 7 recorded live songs, per the previously created variable, as an indicator that live songs are representative of a live album recording, rather than a one off recording.
Using the new binary indicator of live/studio, we matched tracks by track name and artist name. This yielded multiple matches for a single song. For instance, seven live recordings of “Folsom Prison Blues” exist in the data set, and four studio recordings (Mercury Albums, Total Johnny Cash Sun Collection, All About the Blue Train, and I Walk the Line), giving us 28 possible matches to compare among Live to Studio. To cull the data for the project, we scraped the “popularity index” from our original artist list, and kept only the tracks with the highest popularity index. Using this new, parsed down, matched list of live and studio versions, we calculated the difference of audio features (acoustics, duration, instrumentals) from the live to studio version for each track.

Introducing the
LIVE MUSIC
ANALYST
by Kat Wilson and Kevin Litman-Navarro
It’s been a long time since we’ve seen live music. Of course, with modern streaming platforms, there’s more than enough recorded music to keep us safely locked down ad infinitum; yet there remains a deficiency in our musical diets amidst the plague of cancelled shows and closed venues.
What exactly do we miss? Is it the random banter outside of the lyrics we know by heart? A slow jam revived as an up-tempo frenzy? The spontaneous, five-minute guitar solos? A banger gone acoustic? Or the solidarity of strangers in the audience who love that band as much as you do? Maybe it’s the surrounding context of the show (Johnny Cash’s prison performances, Nirvana’s intimate NYC acoustic set, or LCD Soundsystem’s “final goodbye” Madison Square Garden show), that give us insight into what was going on with the audience, the artist, and the world, at the time of the performance.
In the time before we can go back to crowding Brooklyn Steel or catching an intimate set at Hole in the Wall, we decided to dive into the vast discography of live-recorded albums to try and satiate the desire to catch a show. First, we found as many live albums as we could and matched them to their studio counterparts using the SpotifyAPI. Then, by looking at the differences between live and studio songs using numerical metrics like energy (how intense or lively a track sounds), valence (a measurement of a song’s mood), and duration (to find those five-minute guitar solos), we found great live performances that we had missed.
For instance, Bob Dylan’s Blowin’ in the Wind doesn’t exactly come to mind as the encore to end a cross country stadium tour. The folk ballad is typically sung at a slow, ticking rate; it sounds almost like a lullaby. Dylan metronomically recites the lyrics over a simple acoustic strumming pattern, only pausing for a short, intimate, harmonica break in the middle. When analyzing the data, we noticed that the live-recorded version of the song, off of Before the Flood, is, by contrast, a frenzied, five-minute celebration.

Recorded at the Los Angeles Forum during the tail end of Dylan’s 1974 American tour with The Band, the artist (and the audience) take on a new energy. Listen to the difference below.

In this version, fans cheer, and the drums pick up in the background as you hear Dylan’s voice creak over the mic. A guitar solo halfway through replaces Dylan’s studio harmonica, and almost ten seconds of applause linger on as he shouts “Thank you, Goodnight!” It’s as if, over the backdrop of a nation closer to the end of the Vietnam War that first inspired the song, the lyrics take on a different tone.
Other changes are more intentional. David Byrne, for instance, made the choice, when recording three live shows at the Pantages theater in Los Angeles with the Talking Heads, to have each musician and instrument come out onto the stage in succession, one at a time. Byrne was inspired by the minimalist Japanese theater, where stage props and actors were portable, to remove the fourth wall. The resulting performance, captured in the documentary film “Stop Making Sense” brings the audience into the music, creating a type of “build up” approach to sound. You can hear this change in songs like “Heaven,” an acoustic, stripped-down version of the original studio recording.

Levels of speech and instrumentals often seesaw in live performance, too. The iconic saxophone solo in Aretha Franklin’s “Respect,” for example, is certainly not the center of attention, as it is in the studio version. Instead, Aretha’s backup singers take more of a central role. At the Filmore West in San Francisco in 1971, the jam starts out with some stage banter, and the tempo picks up way faster than the studio version. The sax solo is almost “rushed” through, and in its place, backup singers bring even more force to the song.

METHODOLOGY
There are an estimated 10,000 artists who have recorded live albums in recording history. One of our conceptual challenges was figuring out how to get a comprehensive list of artists and albums, while still parsing down the data to create a functional tool. Alas, we might have missed your favorite artist, but hope that we struck some sort of comprehensive list, and encourage you to dig for that underground live version you can’t find here. Our list of artists comes from Wikipedia’s list of live recorded albums, compared to the set of Pop/Rock artists who recorded at least one live recorded album by 9/16/2020, as they appear on AllMusic. We pulled the intersected list of artist names (about 10,950) from the Spotify API, and ended up with around 8,000 artists’ Spotify API data. We culled this list of artists by selecting only artists who had charted on the Billboard Hot 100.
Raw SpotifyAPI data includes song level variables such as acoustics, speech levels, and duration of a song, and album level variables such as album name and year recorded. We hard coded a binary indicator of live/studio by identifying tracks with the string “Live” or “Sessions” in the track name or in the album name. We removed tracks with “Commentary”, “Rehearsals”, “Intro”, “Movie Soundtrack”, or “Demos” from the analysis, and only kept artists who had at least 7 recorded live songs, per the previously created variable, as an indicator that live songs are representative of a live album recording, rather than a one off recording.
Using the new binary indicator of live/studio, we matched tracks by track name and artist name. This yielded multiple matches for a single song. For instance, seven live recordings of “Folsom Prison Blues” exist in the data set, and four studio recordings (Mercury Albums, Total Johnny Cash Sun Collection, All About the Blue Train, and I Walk the Line), giving us 28 possible matches to compare among Live to Studio. To cull the data for the project, we scraped the “popularity index” from our original artist list, and kept only the tracks with the highest popularity index. Using this new, parsed down, matched list of live and studio versions, we calculated the difference of audio features (acoustics, duration, instrumentals) from the live to studio version for each track.
Music is in our hearts, and we will be the first ones back at the venues when they open up again. In the meantime, you can support live music during covid by getting your live performance ready for when the stage opens back, or find other ways to support live musicians.
